kg.node.rt_vertex_stage.desc.1: The vertex half of the shader. It holds the blocks that write per-vertex outputs — right-click the node to add one. A graph whose vertex stage is empty compiles to the vanilla vertex shader, byte for byte.
kg.node.rt_vertex_stage.desc.2: Blocks: Position (model-space vertex position), Normal (model-space normal), glPosition (advanced, clip-space) and Custom Float/Vec2/Vec3/Vec4, which carry a value across to the fragment stage.
kg.node.rt_vertex_stage.note.1: Position, Normal and glPosition can each be added once. Position and glPosition both drive the vertex position, so they cannot be used together.
kg.node.rt_fragment_stage.desc.1: The per-pixel half of the shader. Its blocks write the four semantic outputs the compiler assembles into the final fragColor.
kg.node.rt_fragment_stage.desc.2: Every output you leave out keeps its default — white base color, alpha 1, no emission, no discard — so an empty fragment stage renders solid white.
kg.node.rt_vertex_model_position.desc.1: Replaces the model-space vertex position. Minecraft's standard transform still runs afterwards, so feeding the Position input node straight in is the identity — exactly like Unity's master node.
kg.node.rt_vertex_model_position.desc.2: Left unconnected the block contributes nothing: the emitted GLSL is identical to a graph without it.
kg.node.rt_vertex_model_position.example: Position + Normal * sin(Time) * 0.1 inflates and deflates the mesh along its own normals.
kg.node.rt_vertex_model_position.note.1: The mesh position is in whatever space the vertices were written in: true object space in the preview, Minecraft's pose-baked camera-relative world space in-world. Offsets and normal-based displacement behave the same in both; absolute rotations or scales about the origin do not.
kg.node.rt_vertex_model_normal.desc.1: Replaces the model-space normal for every consumer: the default lit vertex color, the world-normal varying behind Fresnel-style defaults, and the Normal input node.
kg.node.rt_vertex_model_normal.desc.2: Left unconnected the block contributes nothing — the mesh's own Normal attribute flows through.
kg.node.rt_vertex_model_normal.in.normal: The new model-space normal. It need not be unit length; consumers normalize where it matters.
kg.node.rt_vertex_position.desc.1: Advanced. Bypasses the standard transform and writes gl_Position yourself — whatever you wire in becomes the final clip-space position, so the projection is your responsibility.
kg.node.rt_vertex_position.desc.2: Unconnected it emits the vanilla transform, so adding the block alone changes nothing.
kg.node.rt_vertex_position.in.position: The final clip-space position, before the perspective divide.
kg.node.rt_vertex_position.note.1: Mutually exclusive with the Position block: both drive the vertex position, and using them together is a graph error.
kg.node.rt_vertex_custom_float.desc.1: Carries a float from the vertex stage into the fragment stage. The input is evaluated once per vertex, interpolated across the triangle, and read from the matching output port anywhere in the fragment stage.
kg.node.rt_vertex_custom_float.desc.2: Use it to move per-vertex work out of the fragment shader, or to reach vertex-only data — a vertex attribute, gl_VertexID — from a fragment node.
kg.node.rt_vertex_custom_float.out.value: The interpolated value, in the fragment stage.
kg.node.rt_vertex_custom_float.note.1: The fragment sees a blend of the triangle's three vertices, not one vertex's exact value.
kg.node.rt_vertex_custom_vec2.desc.1: Carries a vec2 from the vertex stage into the fragment stage. The input is evaluated once per vertex, interpolated across the triangle, and read from the matching output port anywhere in the fragment stage.
kg.node.rt_vertex_custom_vec2.desc.2: Handy for a uv you want to compute per vertex — distorted texture coordinates, a scrolling offset — instead of per pixel.
kg.node.rt_vertex_custom_vec2.out.value: The interpolated value, in the fragment stage.
kg.node.rt_vertex_custom_vec2.note.1: The fragment sees a blend of the triangle's three vertices, not one vertex's exact value.
kg.node.rt_vertex_custom_vec3.desc.1: Carries a vec3 from the vertex stage into the fragment stage. The input is evaluated once per vertex, interpolated across the triangle, and read from the matching output port anywhere in the fragment stage.
kg.node.rt_vertex_custom_vec3.desc.2: The usual choice for a position or direction computed in the vertex shader, such as a custom-space position the fragment stage needs.
kg.node.rt_vertex_custom_vec3.out.value: The interpolated value, in the fragment stage.
kg.node.rt_vertex_custom_vec3.note.1: Interpolating a direction shortens it; normalize again in the fragment stage if length matters.
kg.node.rt_vertex_custom_vec4.desc.1: Carries a vec4 from the vertex stage into the fragment stage. The input is evaluated once per vertex, interpolated across the triangle, and read from the matching output port anywhere in the fragment stage.
kg.node.rt_vertex_custom_vec4.desc.2: The widest varying — a color with alpha, or four unrelated floats packed together to stay under the driver's varying budget.
kg.node.rt_vertex_custom_vec4.out.value: The interpolated value, in the fragment stage.
kg.node.rt_vertex_custom_vec4.note.1: The fragment sees a blend of the triangle's three vertices, not one vertex's exact value.
kg.node.rt_fragment_base_color.desc.1: Writes the fragment's RGB. Without this block the base color defaults to white, so most graphs start here.
kg.node.rt_fragment_base_color.in.color: The unlit surface color. Not clamped — Emission is added on top afterwards.
kg.node.rt_fragment_base_color.example.1: Sampler Texture 2D into color reproduces a plain textured render type.
kg.node.rt_fragment_base_color.note.1: Color only. Transparency comes from the separate Alpha block.
kg.node.rt_fragment_alpha.desc.1: Writes the fragment's alpha. Without this block alpha defaults to 1.
kg.node.rt_fragment_alpha.note.1: Alpha only reaches the screen if the graph's render settings use a blend mode that reads it; with blending off, a value below 1 changes nothing.
kg.node.rt_fragment_emission.desc.1: Adds light on top of the base color. It is applied after Base Color is written, so it is unaffected by that block's own math.
kg.node.rt_fragment_emission.in.color: The color to add. Not clamped; values above 1 only matter in a pipeline that reads over-bright output.
kg.node.rt_fragment_emission.example.1: Fresnel into Multiply with a color, then into Emission, gives a glowing rim that survives darkness.
kg.node.rt_fragment_alpha_discard.desc.1: Kills the fragment outright when the final alpha falls below the cutoff — the classic cutout/alpha-test look, with hard edges rather than a blend.
kg.node.rt_fragment_alpha_discard.desc.2: The test runs after Emission and against the value the Alpha block produced, so it sees the finished alpha.
kg.node.rt_fragment_alpha_discard.in.cut: Fragments with alpha strictly below this are discarded.
kg.node.rt_fragment_alpha_discard.note.1: Discarding disables early depth testing on most drivers; prefer a blend mode when a soft edge would do.
kg.node.rt_uv.desc.1: The mesh's texture coordinates for the selected channel. Works in both stages: the raw vertex attribute in the vertex shader, the interpolated varying in the fragment shader.
kg.node.rt_uv.desc.2: Most uv-typed input ports already fall back to this when left unconnected, so you only need the node when you want to transform the coordinates before use.
kg.node.rt_uv.out.out: The uv, normally 0..1 across the quad for UV0.
kg.node.rt_uv.option.channel.tooltip.uv0: UV0: the texture coordinate — the one you almost always want.
kg.node.rt_uv.option.channel.tooltip.uv1: UV1: Minecraft's overlay coordinate (damage/hurt tint), constant per draw.
kg.node.rt_uv.option.channel.tooltip.uv2: UV2: Minecraft's lightmap coordinate (block/sky light), constant per draw.
kg.node.rt_uv.note.1: UV1 and UV2 are constant for the whole draw, so their preview is a flat color rather than a gradient.
kg.node.rt_position.desc.1: The surface position of the mesh in the selected space. Works in both stages — the raw vertex position in the vertex shader, the interpolated position in the fragment shader.
kg.node.rt_position.desc.2: Each space is defined by the render pipeline. A pipeline whose vertices carry no object space maps Object onto World.
kg.node.rt_position.out.out: The position in the selected space.
kg.node.rt_position.option.space.tooltip: Object: the per-draw model space the vertices were written in.
World: absolute world coordinates, the same numbers the F3 screen shows.
View: eye space — the camera sits at the origin looking down -Z.
kg.node.rt_position.example.1: Feed World position into Fract to get a 1-block repeating pattern that stays locked to the world grid as the camera moves.
kg.node.rt_position.note.1: Unity's Tangent and Absolute World spaces are not offered: Minecraft meshes carry no per-vertex tangent basis, and World here is already absolute.
kg.node.rt_position.note.2: The node preview has no real vertex stage, so it shows the preview mesh's object position for every space.
kg.node.rt_normal.desc.1: The surface normal of the mesh in the selected space, always normalized (interpolation does not preserve unit length). Works in both stages.
kg.node.rt_normal.desc.2: A Normal block in the vertex stage replaces the source this reads, so displaced geometry can report a matching normal.
kg.node.rt_normal.out.out: The unit-length normal in the selected space.
kg.node.rt_normal.option.space.tooltip.o: Object: model space, straight from the Normal vertex attribute.
kg.node.rt_normal.option.space.tooltip.w: World: rotated into world space — what you want for sky/environment effects.
kg.node.rt_normal.option.space.tooltip.v: View: rotated into eye space — what you want for screen-facing effects.
kg.node.rt_normal.note.1: Minecraft's matrices are pure rotations, so normals use the plain rotation rather than an inverse-transpose.
kg.node.rt_normal.note.2: A mesh whose vertex format has no Normal element degrades to object-space +Y.
kg.node.rt_view_direction.desc.1: The vector from the surface to the camera. By default it is NOT normalized, so its length is the distance to the camera — which is what makes distance fades cheap.
kg.node.rt_view_direction.desc.2: The camera sits at the view-space origin, so the raw direction is simply -viewPos, then rotated into the space you pick. Minecraft's matrices are rotation plus translation, so the length survives the rotation.
kg.node.rt_view_direction.out.out: The direction, unit length only when the normalize option is on.
kg.node.rt_view_direction.option.space.t: World: the direction in world space.
Object: the direction rotated into the mesh's model space.
View: the direction in eye space.
kg.node.rt_view_direction.example.1: Length of View Direction into Saturate fades a highlight out as the camera walks away.
kg.node.rt_view_direction.note.1: Tangent space is unavailable — Minecraft meshes carry no per-vertex tangent basis.
kg.node.rt_vertex_color.desc.1: The mesh's vertex color, optionally lit. Works in both stages: computed from the raw attributes in the vertex shader, read as an interpolated varying in the fragment shader.
kg.node.rt_vertex_color.desc.2: This is the tint Minecraft itself applies — entity flash, biome grass color, particle color — so multiplying your base color by it keeps a render type behaving like vanilla.
kg.node.rt_vertex_color.note.1: Mix Light needs the Normal and Color attributes; Block needs UV2. A vertex format missing them degrades to unlit color, or to white if Color is absent too.
kg.node.rt_in_vertex_attribute.desc.1: Reads one raw attribute straight out of the vertex format — the vertex shader's in variable, untouched. The dropdown lists every registered element, and the output port re-types itself to match your choice.
kg.node.rt_in_vertex_attribute.desc.2: Use it when you need the attribute exactly as uploaded, before any of the convenience nodes normalize or transform it.
kg.node.rt_in_vertex_attribute.out.out: The attribute value; ivec2 elements such as UV1/UV2 are read as vec2.
kg.node.rt_in_vertex_attribute.note.1: Vertex-only. Pulling it into the fragment stage is a stage error — route it through a Custom varying block instead.
kg.node.rt_in_vertex_attribute.note.2: The graph warns when the chosen element is not part of the current vertex format.
kg.node.rt_vertex_id.desc.1: The index of the current vertex inside the draw call. Handy for giving each vertex, or each quad, its own pseudo-random value.
kg.node.rt_vertex_id.desc.2: Usable in both stages: the fragment stage reads it through an automatically forwarded flat varying, so all three vertices of a triangle report the provoking vertex's id rather than a blend.
kg.node.rt_vertex_id.out.out: The vertex index within the draw.
kg.node.rt_vertex_id.example.1: Floor of Vertex ID / 4 gives a per-quad index for quad geometry — feed it into Random Range for a per-quad seed.
kg.node.rt_vertex_id.note.1: The node preview has no real vertex stage, so it substitutes 0.
kg.node.rt_instance_id.desc.1: The index of the current instance in an instanced draw, and 0 for ordinary draws.
kg.node.rt_instance_id.desc.2: Usable in both stages: the fragment stage reads it through an automatically forwarded flat varying.
kg.node.rt_instance_id.out.out: The instance index, 0 when the draw is not instanced.
kg.node.rt_instance_id.note.1: Minecraft rarely uses instanced draws, so this is usually 0 unless your own pipeline sets it up.
kg.node.rt_fragment_coord.desc.1: The raw window-space coordinate of the fragment: xy is the pixel, z the window-space depth in 0..1, and w is 1 divided by the clip-space w.
kg.node.rt_fragment_coord.desc.2: Distinct from Screen Position, which normalizes xy into uv space and carries no depth. Use this when you want actual pixels — a screen-space dither or scanline pattern that does not stretch with resolution.
kg.node.rt_front_facing.desc.1: Whether this fragment belongs to a front-facing primitive. Pairs with Branch for two-sided shading — a different color, or a flipped normal, on back faces.
kg.node.rt_front_facing.note.1: Only meaningful when back-face culling is off in the graph's render settings; with culling on, back faces never reach the fragment shader.
kg.node.rt_primitive_id.desc.1: The index of the primitive being shaded within the current draw call.
kg.node.rt_primitive_id.note.1: Minecraft batches geometry into few draw calls, so this is the triangle index within the batch rather than a stable per-object id.
The interpolated spherical distance from the camera to the fragment — the same value vanilla fog uses. Reads the varying the vertex stage writes, defaulting to the standard fog distance.
kg.node.rt_frag_cylindrical_distance.des: The interpolated cylindrical distance from the camera to the fragment — horizontal distance combined with height, as vanilla's cylindrical fog uses it.
kg.node.rt_vec2.desc.1: Builds a vec2 from two floats.
kg.node.rt_vec3.desc.1: Builds a vec3 from three floats. The usual way to assemble a color or a direction out of separately computed channels.
kg.node.rt_vec4.desc.1: Builds a vec4 from four floats — a color with alpha, or a homogeneous position.
kg.node.rt_combine.tooltip: Assembles up to four floats into a vec4, vec3 or vec2.
kg.node.rt_split.tooltip: Splits a vector into its four channels as floats.
kg.node.rt_swizzle.tooltip: Rebuilds a vector by picking and reordering the input's channels.
kg.node.rt_flip.tooltip: Mirrors the selected channels around 0.5 (x becomes 1 - x).
kg.node.rt_color.tooltip: A constant color, baked into the shader as a literal.
kg.node.rt_time.tooltip: World time in seconds, updated every frame — the value to animate with.
kg.node.rt_game_time.tooltip: Minecraft's day fraction, wrapping from 0 to 1 each Minecraft day.
kg.node.rt_vec2.tooltip: Builds a vec2 from two floats.
kg.node.rt_vec3.tooltip: Builds a vec3 from three floats.
kg.node.rt_vec4.tooltip: Builds a vec4 from four floats.
kg.node.rt_combine.desc.1: Assembles up to four separate floats into a vector. All three groupings come out at once, so one node covers vec4, vec3 and vec2 without rewiring.
kg.node.rt_combine.note.1: Unconnected channels are 0, so a partly wired Combine gives black rather than white.
kg.node.rt_split.desc.1: Breaks a vector into its four channels as separate floats — the mirror image of Combine.
kg.node.rt_split.desc.2: The input is dynamic, so a narrower vector reads its missing channels as 0: splitting a vec2 gives b = a = 0.
kg.node.rt_split.out.b: Channel 2 — blue, or z; 0 when the input is narrower.
kg.node.rt_split.out.a: Channel 3 — alpha, or w; 0 when the input is narrower.
kg.node.rt_split.example.1: Split a sampled texture and route its alpha into the Alpha block while its rgb goes to Base Color.
kg.node.rt_swizzle.desc.1: Rebuilds a vector by picking, reordering or repeating the input's channels. Each of the four slots chooses a source channel (x/y/z/w) or - for none.
kg.node.rt_swizzle.desc.2: The output width is the number of leading slots that are not -, so x,y,-,- gives a vec2. Channels the input does not have read as 0.
kg.node.rt_swizzle.out.out: The rebuilt vector; its width follows the slots.
kg.node.rt_swizzle.example.1: Slots z,y,x,w turn an RGBA color into BGRA. Slots x,x,x,- broadcasts one channel into a grayscale vec3.
kg.node.rt_flip.desc.1: Mirrors the selected channels around 0.5, mapping x to 1 - x and leaving the other channels alone. Mostly used on uv coordinates.
kg.node.rt_flip.in.in: The vector to flip; only the channels it actually has are considered.
kg.node.rt_flip.out.out: The flipped vector, same width as the input.
kg.node.rt_flip.example.1: Flip the y channel of a UV node to fix a texture that reads upside down.
kg.node.rt_flip.note.1: The formula assumes the 0..1 range. Flipping a value outside it mirrors around 0.5 all the same, which is rarely what you want.
kg.node.rt_color.desc.1: A fixed color, edited with the ARGB picker and baked into the shader as a literal. It costs nothing at runtime because it is a constant.
kg.node.rt_color.out.color: The color as a vec4, with each channel in 0..1.
kg.node.rt_color.note.1: Constant, not adjustable at runtime. For a color you want to change per material, expose a global graph variable instead — that compiles to a uniform.
kg.node.rt_time.desc.1: World time in seconds, updated every frame by KilaGraph. This is the value to drive animations with.
kg.node.rt_time.example.1: Time * 0.5 into a Tiling And Offset node's offset scrolls a texture at half a tile per second.
kg.node.rt_time.note.1: It keeps growing, so a raw multiply eventually loses float precision. Wrap it with Fract or Mod for anything long-running.
kg.node.rt_game_time.desc.1: Minecraft's own day fraction: a value in 0..1 that wraps every Minecraft day of 24000 ticks.
kg.node.rt_game_time.out.gameTime: The day fraction, wrapping back to 0 each day.
kg.node.rt_game_time.note.1: For smooth animation use the Time node instead — this one jumps back to 0 at dawn and is far too slow for most effects.
kg.node.rt_gradient.desc.1: A fixed gradient: color keys and alpha keys on their own tracks, with Blend or Fixed interpolation, baked into the shader.
kg.node.rt_gradient.desc.2: It is an opaque value, not a color. Feed it into a Sample Gradient node together with a position to actually get a color out.
kg.node.rt_gradient.out.gradient: The gradient value, for a Sample Gradient node.
kg.node.rt_gradient.note.1: Constant. For a gradient you want to change at runtime, expose a graph variable of type Gradient instead.
kg.node.rt_curve.desc.1: A fixed float curve: cubic bezier segments drawn in the curve editor, remapped to the range you set, and baked into the shader.
kg.node.rt_curve.desc.2: It is an opaque value, not a number. Feed it into a Sample Curve node together with a position to get a float out.
kg.node.rt_curve.out.curve: The curve value, for a Sample Curve node.
kg.node.rt_curve.example.1: A curve that eases in and out turns a linear Time into a natural-looking pulse.
kg.node.rt_curve.note.1: Constant. For a curve you want to change at runtime, expose a graph variable of type Curve instead.
kg.node.rt_branch.desc.1: Picks one of two values based on a boolean. Both are still computed — this selects a result, it does not skip work.
kg.node.rt_branch.desc.2: The two operands are dynamic and are widened to whichever is broader, and the output carries that width.
kg.node.rt_branch.in.t: Used when the predicate is true.
kg.node.rt_branch.in.f: Used when the predicate is false.
kg.node.rt_branch.example.1: Front Facing into predicate, with two different colors on t and f, shades the two sides of a plane differently.
kg.node.rt_branch.note.1: For real control flow — an if that actually skips work, or a loop — use the Expression node and write the GLSL yourself.
kg.node.rt_compare.desc.1: Compares two numbers with the selected operator and gives a boolean, ready for a Branch predicate.
kg.node.rt_compare.option.op.tooltip: The comparison to apply between a and b.
kg.node.rt_compare.note.1: Scalar only, like Unity. Equality on floats is unreliable — prefer a less-than test on the distance between the two values.
kg.node.rt_and.desc.1: Boolean and: true only when both inputs are true.
kg.node.rt_or.desc.1: Boolean or: true when either input is true.
kg.node.rt_expression.desc.1: A node you write yourself in GLSL. Declare any number of typed inputs and outputs plus a body, and the node compiles to a helper function the shader calls — Unity's Custom Function node, in string mode.
kg.node.rt_expression.desc.2: The body reads each input by its port name and writes each output by its port name. Editing the spec re-defines the node's ports immediately.
kg.node.rt_expression.desc.3: This is also the only way to express real control flow. If, for and while cannot be drawn as wires in a flat-expression compiler, so anything that must gate or repeat work belongs here.
kg.node.rt_expression.example.1: Inputs a (VEC3) and n (FLOAT), output result (VEC3), body: result = a; for (int i = 0; i < int(n); i++) result = result * a;
kg.node.rt_expression.note.1: Port names become GLSL identifiers verbatim, so avoid reserved words such as in, out or float — a bad name shows up as a compile error in the preview panel.
kg.node.rt_expression.note.2: Sampler2D can be an input but never an output.
kg.node.rt_add.desc.1: Adds the two inputs channel by channel. Adding a float to a vector adds it to every channel.
kg.node.rt_subtract.desc.1: Subtracts b from a channel by channel.
kg.node.rt_multiply.desc.1: Multiplies the two inputs channel by channel — the usual way to tint a color or scale a uv.
kg.node.rt_multiply.note.1: This is not a dot or matrix product. Use Dot Product, or the Matrix nodes, for those.
kg.node.rt_divide.desc.1: Divides a by b channel by channel.
kg.node.rt_divide.note.1: Dividing by 0 gives inf or NaN, which usually shows up as a black or white pixel. Guard the divisor with Max if it can reach zero.
kg.node.rt_pow.desc.1: Raises a to the power b channel by channel. A common way to sharpen a 0..1 mask: higher exponents push it toward 0.
kg.node.rt_pow.note.1: GLSL's pow is undefined for a negative base; feed it non-negative values.
kg.node.rt_sqrt.desc.1: Square root channel by channel. On a 0..1 mask it does the opposite of Pow: it lifts values toward 1.
kg.node.rt_abs.desc.1: Drops the sign of each channel. Folding a signed value with Abs is the usual way to make a symmetric shape out of a coordinate.
kg.node.rt_negate.desc.1: Flips the sign of each channel.
kg.node.rt_inversesqrt.desc.1: One over the square root of each channel — the hardware has a fast instruction for this, so it beats a Sqrt followed by a Reciprocal.
kg.node.rt_exp.tooltip: Exponential with a selectable base, component-wise.
kg.node.rt_exp.desc.1: Raises the chosen base to the power of the input, channel by channel.
kg.node.rt_exp.option.base.tooltip.2: 2: exp2(a), which the hardware computes directly.
kg.node.rt_log.tooltip: Logarithm with a selectable base, component-wise.
kg.node.rt_log.desc.1: The logarithm of the input in the chosen base, channel by channel.
kg.node.rt_log.option.base.tooltip: Which base to take the logarithm in.
kg.node.rt_log.option.base.tooltip.2: 2: log2(a), which the hardware computes directly.
kg.node.rt_mod.desc.1: The remainder after dividing a by b. Unlike C, GLSL's mod follows the sign of the divisor, so mod(-0.25, 1) is 0.75 — which is what makes it useful for wrapping coordinates.
kg.node.rt_length.tooltip: length(v): the magnitude of a vector.
kg.node.rt_length.desc.1: The straight-line length of the vector. Length of a View Direction gives the distance to the camera.
kg.node.rt_normalize.tooltip: normalize(v): scales a vector to unit length.
kg.node.rt_normalize.desc.1: Keeps the direction, sets the length to 1. Interpolated normals and directions are not unit length, so normalize them before a dot product.
kg.node.rt_posterize.tooltip: Quantises the input into a fixed number of bands.
kg.node.rt_posterize.desc.1: Snaps each channel down to the nearest of steps evenly spaced levels — the poster/cel-shading look.
kg.node.rt_posterize.in.in: The value to quantise, usually in 0..1.
kg.node.rt_posterize.in.steps: How many bands. Higher means a finer staircase.
kg.node.rt_posterize.example.1: Lighting into Posterize with steps 4 gives banded cel shading.
kg.node.rt_ceil.desc.1: Rounds each channel up to the next whole number.
kg.node.rt_floor.desc.1: Rounds each channel down. Paired with Fract it splits a coordinate into a cell index and a position inside that cell — the basis of most tiling effects.
kg.node.rt_round.tooltip: round(a): rounds to the nearest whole number, component-wise.
kg.node.rt_round.desc.1: Rounds each channel to the nearest integer.
kg.node.rt_truncate.desc.1: Drops the fractional part, rounding toward zero — so -1.7 becomes -1, not -2.
kg.node.rt_sign.desc.1: Reports which side of zero each channel is on.
kg.node.rt_step.tooltip: step(edge, x): 0 below the edge, 1 at or above it.
kg.node.rt_step.desc.1: A hard threshold with no branching.
kg.node.rt_step.in.b: The value being tested; the result is 1 once it reaches the edge.
kg.node.rt_step.example.1: Step with edge 0.5 on a noise texture turns it into a crisp black-and-white mask.
kg.node.rt_step.note.1: The hard edge aliases badly. Smoothstep, or a Step whose edge width comes from DDXY, gives a cleaner line.
kg.node.rt_clamp.tooltip: clamp(value, min, max): keeps a value inside a range.
kg.node.rt_clamp.desc.1: Constrains each channel into the range, component-wise.
kg.node.rt_saturate.tooltip: clamp(a, 0, 1): keeps a value inside the unit range.
kg.node.rt_saturate.desc.1: The 0..1 clamp, which most color and mask math wants. Free on most hardware, so use it rather than a general Clamp when the range is 0..1.
kg.node.rt_fract.desc.1: Keeps only what is after the decimal point, so any input wraps into 0..1. This is how you tile a coordinate.
kg.node.rt_fract.example.1: Fract of a uv multiplied by 4 repeats a texture four times across the surface.
kg.node.rt_min.desc.1: The smaller of the two per channel. On masks it acts as an intersection.
kg.node.rt_max.desc.1: The larger of the two per channel. On masks it acts as a union, and it is the cheap way to keep a value away from zero before a divide.
kg.node.rt_one_minus.desc.1: Inverts a 0..1 value — the standard way to flip a mask.
kg.node.rt_remap.tooltip: Linearly remaps a value from one range into another.
kg.node.rt_remap.desc.1: Rescales the input so that inMin lands on outMin and inMax lands on outMax, keeping everything in between proportional.
kg.node.rt_remap.in.outMin: Value the input range's start maps to.
kg.node.rt_remap.in.outMax: Value the input range's end maps to.
kg.node.rt_remap.example.1: Remapping a -1..1 sine into 0..1 makes it usable as a mask or a color.
kg.node.rt_remap.note.1: Nothing is clamped: an input outside its range extrapolates past the output range. Follow with Saturate if you need it bounded.
kg.node.rt_random_range.tooltip: A deterministic pseudo-random value between min and max.
kg.node.rt_random_range.desc.1: Hashes the seed into a value in the range. The same seed always gives the same result — it is not animated unless you feed time into the seed.
kg.node.rt_random_range.in.seed: The hash input. A uv gives per-pixel noise; a per-quad index gives one value per quad.
kg.node.rt_random_range.note.1: The classic sine-based hash. It is cheap but shows visible patterns on large coordinates; the Simple Noise node is better for texture-like randomness.
kg.node.rt_lerp.tooltip: mix(a, b, t): blends from a to b by t.
kg.node.rt_lerp.desc.1: Linear interpolation. t of 0 gives a, 1 gives b, and values between blend proportionally. The workhorse for mixing two colors by a mask.
kg.node.rt_lerp.note.1: t is not clamped, so values outside 0..1 extrapolate past a and b.
kg.node.rt_inverse_lerp.tooltip: The inverse of Lerp: which t maps a and b onto the given value.
kg.node.rt_inverse_lerp.desc.1: Answers the question Lerp asks in reverse: given a, b and a value t between them, what blend factor produced it. Feeding the result back into Lerp with the same a and b returns the original.
kg.node.rt_smoothstep.tooltip: smoothstep(edge0, edge1, x): a smooth 0-to-1 ramp between two edges.
kg.node.rt_smoothstep.desc.1: Like Step, but with a soft, S-curved transition between the two edges instead of a hard jump — and clamped outside them.
kg.node.rt_smoothstep.example.1: Feeding a distance into Smoothstep with edges at radius and radius plus a little gives a soft-edged circle.
kg.node.rt_smoothstep.note.1: When edge0 equals edge1 the result is undefined; keep a gap between them.
kg.node.rt_sin.desc.1: The sine wave, oscillating between -1 and 1 with a period of 2 pi. Remap it into 0..1 to use it as a mask.
kg.node.rt_cos.desc.1: The cosine wave — the same shape as sine, shifted a quarter period.
kg.node.rt_tan.desc.1: The tangent. It blows up to infinity every half period, so clamp the result if it feeds anything visible.
kg.node.rt_arcsine.desc.1: The angle whose sine is the input. Defined only for inputs in -1..1.
kg.node.rt_arccosine.desc.1: The angle whose cosine is the input. Defined only for inputs in -1..1 — handy for turning a dot product of unit vectors back into an angle.
kg.node.rt_arctangent.desc.1: The angle whose tangent is the input, in -pi/2..pi/2.
kg.node.rt_atan2.tooltip: atan(a, b): the angle of the vector (b, a), in radians.
kg.node.rt_atan2.desc.1: The two-argument arctangent. Unlike plain Arctangent it knows which quadrant the point is in, so it covers the full -pi..pi turn — that is what makes it the right tool for converting a coordinate into an angle.
kg.node.rt_tanh.desc.1: The hyperbolic tangent — an S-curve that squashes any input into -1..1, useful for taming an unbounded value.
kg.node.rt_degrees_to_radians.desc.1: Every trigonometry node here works in radians, so run a degree value through this first.
kg.node.rt_radians_to_degrees.desc.1: The reverse conversion, mostly for making an angle readable.
kg.node.rt_ddx.tooltip: dFdx(a): how fast a changes across the screen's x axis.
kg.node.rt_ddx.desc.1: The screen-space derivative in x. The GPU shades pixels in 2x2 blocks, so this is the difference between the two horizontal neighbours in the block.
kg.node.rt_ddx.note.1: Fragment-only, and the result is constant within each 2x2 pixel block.
kg.node.rt_ddy.tooltip: dFdy(a): how fast a changes across the screen's y axis.
kg.node.rt_ddy.desc.1: The screen-space derivative in y, the vertical counterpart of DDX.
kg.node.rt_ddy.note.1: Fragment-only, and the result is constant within each 2x2 pixel block.
kg.node.rt_ddxy.tooltip: fwidth(a): the total screen-space rate of change.
kg.node.rt_ddxy.desc.1: The sum of the absolute x and y derivatives — roughly how much the value changes over one pixel. This is the standard way to size an anti-aliased edge.
kg.node.rt_ddxy.example.1: Smoothstep with edges at 0.5 minus fwidth and 0.5 plus fwidth turns a hard threshold into a pixel-width anti-aliased line at any zoom.
kg.node.rt_dot.tooltip: dot(a, b): the dot product, a single number.
kg.node.rt_dot.desc.1: Measures how much two vectors point the same way. For unit vectors it is the cosine of the angle between them: 1 when aligned, 0 when perpendicular, -1 when opposed.
kg.node.rt_dot.example.1: Dot of the surface Normal with a light direction is the basic diffuse lighting term.
kg.node.rt_cross.tooltip: cross(a, b): a vector perpendicular to both inputs.
kg.node.rt_cross.desc.1: The cross product. Its direction is perpendicular to the plane of the two inputs, and its length is the area of the parallelogram they span.
kg.node.rt_distance.tooltip: distance(a, b): the straight-line distance between two points.
kg.node.rt_distance.desc.1: The length of the vector from a to b.
kg.node.rt_reflect.tooltip: reflect(i, n): mirrors a direction about a normal.
kg.node.rt_reflect.desc.1: Bounces the incident direction off a surface with the given normal — the basis of mirror and environment reflections.
kg.node.rt_reflect.in.i: The incoming direction, pointing at the surface.
kg.node.rt_reflect.in.n: The surface normal; it should be unit length.
kg.node.rt_project.tooltip: The part of a that lies along b.
kg.node.rt_project.desc.1: Projects a onto b: the shadow a casts on b's direction, as a vector.
kg.node.rt_reject.tooltip: The part of a that is perpendicular to b.
kg.node.rt_reject.desc.1: The rejection — what is left of a after removing its projection onto b. Project plus Reject reconstructs the original vector.
kg.node.rt_fresnel.tooltip: Rim factor: brightest where the surface turns away from the camera.
kg.node.rt_fresnel.desc.1: The Fresnel term. It is near 0 where the surface faces you and rises toward 1 at grazing angles, which is what draws a glow around a silhouette.
kg.node.rt_fresnel.desc.2: Both normal and viewDir are optional: leave them unconnected and the node uses the mesh's own world normal and view direction, so it produces a rim straight out of the box.
kg.node.rt_fresnel.in.normal: Surface normal; unconnected falls back to the mesh normal.
kg.node.rt_fresnel.in.viewDir: Direction to the camera; unconnected falls back to the mesh view direction.
kg.node.rt_fresnel.in.power: Falloff exponent. Higher values tighten the rim to the very edge.
kg.node.rt_fresnel.example.1: Fresnel into Multiply with a color, then into the Emission block, gives the classic glowing outline.
kg.node.rt_fresnel.note.1: It is invisible on a flat quad, which is why this node's preview defaults to a sphere.
kg.node.rt_rotate_about_axis.tooltip: Rotates a vector around an arbitrary axis.
kg.node.rt_rotate_about_axis.desc.1: Rodrigues' rotation formula: spins the input around the axis by the given angle. The axis is normalized for you.
kg.node.rt_rotate_about_axis.in.axis: The axis to rotate around; it does not need to be unit length.
kg.node.rt_sphere_mask.tooltip: A soft spherical mask around a center point.
kg.node.rt_sphere_mask.desc.1: 1 inside the radius, falling off to 0 outside it. Works in any number of dimensions — feed it a uv for a circle, or a world position for a sphere.
kg.node.rt_sphere_mask.in.hardness: 0 for a long soft falloff, approaching 1 for a hard edge.
kg.node.rt_transform.desc.1: Moves a vector between coordinate spaces — Unity's Transform node, adapted to the matrices Minecraft actually provides.
kg.node.rt_transform.desc.2: The type matters as much as the spaces: a position carries the translation, a direction ignores it, and a normal ignores it and comes back normalized.
kg.node.rt_transform.option.from.tooltip: View: eye space, camera at the origin.
Clip: after the projection, before the perspective divide.
kg.node.rt_transform.option.to.tooltip.v: View: eye space, camera at the origin.
kg.node.rt_transform.option.to.tooltip.c: Clip: after the projection, before the perspective divide.
kg.node.rt_transform.option.to.tooltip.s: Screen: clip space with the perspective divide applied.
kg.node.rt_transform.option.type.tooltip: Normal: ignores translation and normalizes the result.
kg.node.rt_transform.note.1: Tangent space is unavailable — Minecraft meshes carry no per-vertex tangent basis.
kg.node.rt_mat4_construct.tooltip: Builds a mat4 from four vec4 columns.
kg.node.rt_mat4_construct.desc.1: Assembles a matrix column by column, matching GLSL's column-major layout.
kg.node.rt_mat4_split.tooltip: Splits a mat4 into its four vec4 columns.
kg.node.rt_mat4_multiply.tooltip: a * b: the matrix product of two mat4s.
kg.node.rt_mat4_multiply.desc.1: Combines two transforms. Order matters: a * b applies b first, then a.
kg.node.rt_mat4_transform.tooltip: m * v: transforms a vec4 by a mat4.
kg.node.rt_mat4_transform.desc.1: Applies the matrix to the vector. Use w = 1 for a position and w = 0 for a direction.
kg.node.rt_mat4_transpose.tooltip: transpose(m): flips a matrix about its diagonal.
kg.node.rt_mat4_transpose.desc.1: Swaps rows and columns. For a pure rotation the transpose is also the inverse, and far cheaper.
kg.node.rt_mat4_inverse.tooltip: inverse(m): the inverse of a mat4.
kg.node.rt_mat4_inverse.note.1: Expensive in a shader, and undefined when the matrix is singular. If m is a rotation, use Transpose instead.
kg.node.rt_mat4_determinant.tooltip: determinant(m): the scalar determinant of a mat4.
kg.node.rt_mat4_determinant.desc.1: How much the matrix scales volume; 0 means it is singular and has no inverse.
kg.node.rt_sawtooth_wave.tooltip: A ramp from -1 to 1 with period 1.
kg.node.rt_sawtooth_wave.desc.1: Rises linearly then snaps back. Period 1, so feed it time multiplied by the frequency you want.
kg.node.rt_triangle_wave.tooltip: A triangle wave in -1..1 with period 1.
kg.node.rt_triangle_wave.desc.1: Rises and falls linearly — a sine's shape without the curve, and cheaper.
kg.node.rt_square_wave.desc.1: A hard on/off oscillation. Useful for blinking, and for stripes when driven by a coordinate rather than time.
kg.node.rt_noise_sine_wave.tooltip: A sine wave jittered by pseudo-random noise.
kg.node.rt_noise_sine_wave.desc.1: sin(in) plus a hashed random term, giving a wobbling wave rather than a clean one.
kg.node.rt_noise_sine_wave.in.minMax: The range the noise term is drawn from: x is the minimum, y the maximum.
kg.node.rt_tiling_offset.desc.1: Scales and shifts a uv: multiply by tiling to repeat the texture, add offset to slide it. The starting point for almost every uv effect.
kg.node.rt_tiling_offset.desc.2: Both uv and tiling have useful defaults — the mesh uv and (1,1) — so the node does something sensible with nothing wired in.
kg.node.rt_tiling_offset.in.uv: Coordinates to transform; unconnected uses the mesh uv.
kg.node.rt_tiling_offset.in.tiling: How many times the texture repeats on each axis.
kg.node.rt_tiling_offset.in.offset: How far to slide the coordinates.
kg.node.rt_tiling_offset.example.1: Tiling (4,4) with Time into offset scrolls a texture that repeats four times across the surface.
kg.node.rt_tiling_offset.note.1: Repeating only works if the sampler's wrap mode is Repeat. Set it on the Texture node, or the edge pixel will smear instead.
kg.node.rt_rotate.desc.1: Spins the uv around a center point. Because the coordinates rotate rather than the image, the visible result turns the opposite way from the angle's sign.
kg.node.rt_rotate.in.uv: Coordinates to rotate; unconnected uses the mesh uv.
kg.node.rt_rotate.in.center: Pivot, in uv space. The default (0.5, 0.5) is the middle of the quad.
kg.node.rt_rotate.in.rotation: The angle, in the unit selected below.
kg.node.rt_rotate.option.unit.tooltip: Whether rotation is read as radians or degrees.
kg.node.rt_rotate.example.1: Time into rotation makes the texture spin at one radian per second.
kg.node.rt_twirl.desc.1: A swirl: the further a pixel sits from the center, the more its coordinates are rotated, so straight lines curl into spirals.
kg.node.rt_twirl.in.uv: Coordinates to distort; unconnected uses the mesh uv.
kg.node.rt_twirl.in.strength: How much extra rotation each unit of distance adds.
kg.node.rt_twirl.in.offset: A shift applied after the swirl.
kg.node.rt_spherize.desc.1: A fisheye bulge: coordinates are pushed outward by the fourth power of their distance from the center, so the middle magnifies and the edges compress.
kg.node.rt_spherize.in.uv: Coordinates to distort; unconnected uses the mesh uv.
kg.node.rt_spherize.in.offset: A shift applied after the distortion.
kg.node.rt_spherize.example.1: A gentle Spherize on a flat quad sells it as a glass bead or a bubble.
kg.node.rt_radial_shear.desc.1: A wave-like shear perpendicular to the radius: coordinates are dragged sideways around the center, growing with the square of the distance.
kg.node.rt_radial_shear.in.uv: Coordinates to distort; unconnected uses the mesh uv.
kg.node.rt_radial_shear.in.strength: How far the coordinates are dragged.
kg.node.rt_radial_shear.in.offset: A shift applied after the distortion.
kg.node.rt_polar_coordinates.desc.1: Converts a uv into polar form around a center: x becomes the distance from the center and y becomes the angle around it.
kg.node.rt_polar_coordinates.desc.2: Sampling a texture with the result wraps it into a ring, which is how radial wipes, sonar sweeps and vortex effects are usually built.
kg.node.rt_polar_coordinates.in.uv: Coordinates to convert; unconnected uses the mesh uv.
kg.node.rt_polar_coordinates.in.center: The pole everything is measured from.
kg.node.rt_polar_coordinates.note.1: The angle wraps from 1 back to 0 on one side of the center; a texture sampled across that line shows a visible seam.
kg.node.rt_flipbook.desc.1: Remaps a uv into a single cell of a sprite sheet, so one texture can hold a whole animation. Drive tile from Time to play it.
kg.node.rt_flipbook.in.uv: Coordinates within the cell; unconnected uses the mesh uv.
kg.node.rt_flipbook.in.width: Number of columns in the sheet.
kg.node.rt_flipbook.in.height: Number of rows in the sheet.
kg.node.rt_flipbook.in.tile: Which cell to show. It wraps automatically, so a value that keeps growing simply loops.
kg.node.rt_flipbook.option.invertX.toolt: Traverse the columns right to left.
kg.node.rt_flipbook.option.invertY.toolt: Traverse the rows bottom to top.
kg.node.rt_flipbook.example.1: Floor of Time * 12 into tile plays a 4x4 sheet at twelve frames a second.
kg.node.rt_flipbook.note.1: Cells bleed into each other when the sampler filters across their edges. Point filtering, or a sheet with padding, avoids it.
kg.node.rt_triplanar.desc.1: Projects a texture onto the surface along all three world axes and blends the three samples by the normal — so geometry gets a consistent texture with no uv at all, and no stretching or seams.
kg.node.rt_triplanar.desc.2: Unconnected position and normal default to the mesh's model-space position and world normal, and an unconnected texture falls back to the missing-texture sampler.
kg.node.rt_triplanar.in.position: Point being textured; unconnected uses the mesh position.
kg.node.rt_triplanar.in.normal: Surface normal driving the blend; unconnected uses the mesh normal.
kg.node.rt_triplanar.in.blend: Sharpness of the transition between the three projections.
kg.node.rt_triplanar.note.1: Three texture fetches per pixel instead of one.
kg.node.rt_triplanar.note.2: The default position is model space while the default normal is world space. That agrees for an unrotated mesh; wire matching-space inputs if the mesh rotates.
kg.node.rt_triplanar.note.3: Fragment-only, since it samples a texture.
kg.node.rt_texture.desc.1: Names a texture and its sampler settings. The compiler bakes it into the material as its own sampler uniform, so this is a constant with no runtime cost.
kg.node.rt_texture.desc.2: It outputs a sampler handle rather than a color — feed it into Sampler Texture 2D to actually read a pixel.
kg.node.rt_texture.note.1: Filter and wrap live in this node's settings, not on the sampling node — set Repeat here if you plan to tile the coordinates.
kg.node.rt_sampler_texture2d.desc.1: Reads a pixel out of a sampler at the given coordinates. The one node that turns a texture into a color.
kg.node.rt_sampler_texture2d.in.sampler: Where to read from; unconnected falls back to the missing-texture checkerboard.
kg.node.rt_sampler_texture2d.in.uv: Where to read; unconnected uses the mesh uv.
kg.node.rt_sampler_texture2d.example.1: Texture into sampler, and Sampler Texture 2D into Base Color, reproduces an ordinary textured render type.
kg.node.rt_overlay_texture.desc.1: Minecraft's overlay sampler — the red flash on a hurt entity and the white flash on a creeper about to explode.
kg.node.rt_overlay_texture.desc.2: Using this node tells the runtime to bind vanilla's overlay texture. Sample it with the UV1 channel.
kg.node.rt_lightmap_texture.desc.1: Minecraft's lightmap sampler — the baked block and sky light that gives world geometry its lighting.
kg.node.rt_lightmap_texture.desc.2: Using this node tells the runtime to bind vanilla's lightmap. Sample it with the UV2 channel and multiply the result into your base color.
kg.node.rt_lightmap_texture.note.1: The Vertex Color node's Block mode already does this for you; reach for this node only when you want the lightmap on its own.
kg.node.rt_screen_position.desc.1: Where this fragment sits on the screen, in the coordinate space you pick. The default mode is the canonical uv to feed Scene Color and Scene Depth.
kg.node.rt_screen_position.out.out: The screen position; which channels are meaningful depends on the mode.
kg.node.rt_screen_position.note.1: Fragment-only. Because it is screen-space, anything built on it slides across the surface as the camera moves.
kg.node.rt_screen.desc.1: The viewport size in pixels. Use it to correct for aspect ratio, or to turn a pixel measurement into a fraction of the screen.
kg.node.rt_screen.example.1: Dividing Width by Height gives the aspect ratio, which keeps a screen-space circle round instead of oval.
kg.node.rt_scene_color.desc.1: The color of the opaque scene already drawn behind this fragment. This is what makes refraction, heat haze and frosted glass possible.
kg.node.rt_scene_color.desc.2: Offsetting the uv slightly before sampling is exactly how a refraction distortion is built: the surface shows the world behind it, displaced.
kg.node.rt_scene_color.in.uv: Screen-space coordinates to read; unconnected uses this fragment's own screen position.
kg.node.rt_scene_color.out.out: The scene color behind this fragment.
kg.node.rt_scene_color.note.1: Only meaningful for a translucent material. The capture is taken after all opaque geometry, so an opaque material draws before the capture exists and reads nothing.
kg.node.rt_scene_color.note.2: The editor preview shows black — the capture happens during the world render, which does not run behind the offscreen preview scene. It is correct in-world.
kg.node.rt_scene_depth.desc.1: How far away the opaque scene behind this fragment is. Comparing it against the fragment's own depth is what softens the edge where a particle or a water plane meets solid geometry.
kg.node.rt_scene_depth.in.uv: Screen-space coordinates to read; unconnected uses this fragment's own screen position.
kg.node.rt_scene_depth.out.out: The depth, in the units the sampling mode implies.
kg.node.rt_scene_depth.example.1: Saturate of the difference between Scene Depth in eye mode and Screen Position raw's w, divided by a fade distance, gives the classic soft-particle fade.
kg.node.rt_scene_depth.note.1: Only meaningful for a translucent material, for the same reason as Scene Color.
kg.node.rt_scene_depth.note.2: The editor preview shows a flat value — there is no scene depth behind the offscreen preview. It is correct in-world.
kg.node.rt_camera.desc.1: The current camera's position, orientation and clip planes — Unity's Camera node.
kg.node.rt_camera.out.Position: Absolute world position of the camera.
kg.node.rt_camera.out.Direction: The direction the camera looks, in world space.
kg.node.rt_camera.out.Up: The camera's up axis, in world space.
kg.node.rt_camera.out.Right: The camera's right axis, in world space.
kg.node.rt_camera.out.Orthographic: 1 for an orthographic projection, 0 for perspective.
kg.node.rt_camera.out.NearPlane: Near clip distance in world units.
kg.node.rt_camera.out.FarPlane: Far clip distance in world units.
kg.node.rt_camera.out.ZBufferSign: 1 in this pipeline: depth grows away from the camera.
kg.node.rt_camera.example.1: Camera Right and Up let a quad face the camera without any billboarding on the CPU side.
kg.node.rt_camera.note.1: Position is reassembled from KilaGraph's precision-split camera uniforms, so it stays accurate far from the world origin.
kg.node.rt_globals_ubo.desc.1: Minecraft's global shader uniforms, straight from the source. Most of these have a friendlier node — Camera, Screen, Game Time — so reach for this one when you need something they do not expose.
kg.node.rt_globals_ubo.out.CameraBlockPo: Integer block part of the camera position, in the precision split.
kg.node.rt_globals_ubo.out.CameraOffset: Fractional part of the camera position, in the precision split.
kg.node.rt_globals_ubo.out.GlintAlpha: Strength of the enchantment glint overlay.
kg.node.rt_globals_ubo.out.MenuBlurRadiu: Blur radius the pause menu is applying.
kg.node.rt_globals_ubo.note.1: Add CameraBlockPos and CameraOffset to get the world camera position — or just use the Camera node, which does it for you.
kg.node.rt_projection_ubo.desc.1: Minecraft's projection matrix, which turns view space into clip space.
kg.node.rt_dynamic_transforms_ubo.desc.1: Minecraft's per-draw transform uniforms — the values vanilla sets before each draw call.
kg.node.rt_dynamic_transforms_ubo.out.Co: The per-draw color tint vanilla multiplies in.
kg.node.rt_dynamic_transforms_ubo.out.Te: Texture coordinate matrix, used by animated render types.
kg.node.rt_kg_transforms_ubo.desc.1: The space-conversion matrices KilaGraph precomputes each draw. They let a graph do its own space math instead of going through the Transform node.
kg.node.rt_kg_transforms_ubo.out.IModelV: View space back to object space.
kg.node.rt_kg_transforms_ubo.out.IViewMa: View space back to world space.
kg.node.rt_kg_transforms_ubo.out.IProjMa: Clip space back to view space.
kg.node.rt_kg_transforms_ubo.note.1: Referencing an output is what declares and binds the matching uniform, so unused matrices cost nothing.
kg.node.rt_kg_transforms_ubo.note.2: The camera's world position is not here — use the Camera node for that.
kg.node.rt_projection_from_position.desc: Applies the projection matrix to a position, taking it into clip space.
kg.node.rt_projection_from_position.in.p: The view-space position; unconnected falls back to the model-space vertex position.
The clip-space position, before the perspective divide.
kg.node.rt_projection_from_position.note: Vertex-only: clip space is a per-vertex concept, and this feeds gl_Position.
kg.node.rt_lighting_ubo.desc.1: The two directional lights vanilla uses for its per-vertex diffuse shading.
kg.node.rt_lighting_ubo.note.1: These are fixed directions in view space, not real world lights — vanilla entity lighting is deliberately simple.
kg.node.rt_mix_light.desc.1: Vanilla's per-vertex diffuse lighting, exposed as a node. This is the shading that used to be hidden inside the Color block; the default entity shader now wires it explicitly so you can edit or remove it.
kg.node.rt_mix_light.in.normal: Surface normal; unconnected uses the Normal vertex attribute.
kg.node.rt_mix_light.in.color: Color to light; unconnected uses the Color vertex attribute.
kg.node.rt_mix_light.note.1: Vertex-only, because its unconnected fallbacks are vertex attributes.
kg.node.rt_apply_fog.desc.1: Blends a color toward the fog color by distance — the last step of a render type that should disappear into the distance like the rest of the world.
kg.node.rt_apply_fog.desc.2: Every input except inColor is optional: unconnected, each falls back to the value vanilla would have used, so wiring only inColor already reproduces vanilla fog.
kg.node.rt_apply_fog.in.sphericalVertexD: Distance driving the fog; unconnected uses the standard fog distance.
kg.node.rt_apply_fog.in.environmentalSta: Distance at which fog begins; unconnected uses vanilla's FogStart.
kg.node.rt_apply_fog.in.environmentalEnd: Distance at which fog is total; unconnected uses vanilla's FogEnd.
kg.node.rt_apply_fog.in.fogColor: Color to fade toward; unconnected uses vanilla's FogColor.
kg.node.rt_apply_fog.note.1: 1.21.1 has a single linear fog band. The cylindrical and render-distance ports are kept for graph compatibility with newer versions but do not affect the result here.
kg.node.rt_fog_ubo.desc.1: Minecraft's fog uniforms, for building a custom fog response instead of using Apply Fog.
kg.node.rt_fog_ubo.out.FogColor: The color the world fades toward.
kg.node.rt_fog_ubo.out.FogRenderDistance: Same band as environmental on this version.
Same band as environmental on this version.
kg.node.rt_fog_ubo.out.FogSkyEnd: Same band as environmental on this version.
kg.node.rt_fog_ubo.out.FogCloudsEnd: Same band as environmental on this version.
kg.node.rt_fog_ubo.note.1: 1.21.1 exposes a single fog band, so the multi-band outputs all report that one band. They exist so a graph stays compatible with newer versions.
kg.node.rt_linear_fog_value.desc.1: How much fog applies at a given distance: 0 before the start, rising to 1 at the end. Use it when you want to drive something other than color with fog.
kg.node.rt_total_fog_value.desc.1: The fog amount for this fragment using the scene's own fog settings — Linear Fog Value with everything filled in for you.
kg.node.rt_total_fog_value.example.1: One Minus of this, multiplied into Alpha, fades a render type out with distance instead of tinting it.
kg.node.rt_fog_spherical_distance.desc.1: Vanilla's spherical fog distance for a position: the straight-line distance from the camera, which is what standard fog uses.
kg.node.rt_fog_spherical_distance.in.pos: The position to measure; unconnected uses the model-space vertex position.
kg.node.rt_fog_spherical_distance.note.1: Vertex-only. Vanilla computes fog distance per vertex and interpolates it; read it in the fragment stage with the Frag Spherical Vertex Distance node.
kg.node.rt_fog_cylindrical_distance.desc: Vanilla's cylindrical fog distance: horizontal distance and height treated separately, which is how the void and nether fogs behave.
kg.node.rt_fog_cylindrical_distance.in.p: The position to measure; unconnected uses the model-space vertex position.
kg.node.rt_checkerboard.desc.1: A two-color checker over the uv. It is derivative-aware, so the squares stay crisp and stop shimmering as they shrink into the distance instead of turning into noise.
kg.node.rt_checkerboard.in.uv: Coordinates; unconnected uses the mesh uv.
kg.node.rt_checkerboard.in.colorA: Color of the first set of squares.
kg.node.rt_checkerboard.in.frequency: How many squares per uv unit on each axis.
kg.node.rt_checkerboard.note.1: Fragment-only, because the anti-aliasing needs screen-space derivatives.
kg.node.rt_simple_noise.desc.1: Soft fractal value noise in 0..1: three octaves of a hashed lattice summed together, so it has both broad shapes and fine detail.
kg.node.rt_simple_noise.in.uv: Coordinates; unconnected uses the mesh uv.
kg.node.rt_simple_noise.in.scale: Base frequency. Higher means smaller features.
kg.node.rt_simple_noise.example.1: Add Time to the uv before the noise and it drifts; multiply the result into Alpha for a dissolving effect.
kg.node.rt_simple_noise.note.1: Value noise is blockier than gradient noise. When you want smooth organic shapes, Gradient Noise is the better choice.
kg.node.rt_gradient_noise.desc.1: Perlin-style gradient noise: random directions at each lattice corner, dotted with the local offset and blended with a quintic fade, then biased into 0..1.
kg.node.rt_gradient_noise.desc.2: Smoother and more organic than Simple Noise, which is why it is the usual starting point for clouds, smoke and flowing distortion.
kg.node.rt_gradient_noise.in.uv: Coordinates; unconnected uses the mesh uv.
kg.node.rt_gradient_noise.example.1: Two Gradient Noises at different scales, one offsetting the other's uv, gives the classic swirling distortion.
kg.node.rt_voronoi.desc.1: Worley noise: one feature point is scattered into each cell of a grid, and every pixel finds its nearest. The result reads as organic cells — cracked mud, scales, stained glass.
kg.node.rt_voronoi.in.uv: Coordinates; unconnected uses the mesh uv.
kg.node.rt_voronoi.in.angleOffset: Jitters where each cell's point sits. Animating it makes the cells crawl.
kg.node.rt_voronoi.in.cellDensity: How many cells fit across a uv unit.
kg.node.rt_voronoi.out.out: Distance to the nearest feature point: 0 at the point, approaching 1 at the cell borders.
kg.node.rt_voronoi.out.cells: A flat random value per cell — a per-region id, useful for coloring each cell differently.
kg.node.rt_voronoi.example.1: One Minus of out, raised to a high power, draws bright veins along the cell borders.
kg.node.rt_ellipse.desc.1: A mask that is 1 inside an axis-aligned ellipse centered on the uv and 0 outside, with a one-pixel anti-aliased edge that holds up at any zoom.
kg.node.rt_ellipse.in.uv: Coordinates; unconnected uses the mesh uv.
kg.node.rt_ellipse.note.1: Fragment-only: the anti-aliased edge is sized with a screen-space derivative.
kg.node.rt_rectangle.desc.1: A mask that is 1 inside an axis-aligned rectangle centered on the uv, with an anti-aliased edge.
kg.node.rt_rectangle.in.uv: Coordinates; unconnected uses the mesh uv.
kg.node.rt_rectangle.note.1: Fragment-only, like the other shape masks.
kg.node.rt_rounded_rectangle.desc.1: A rectangle mask with rounded corners, anti-aliased. The radius is clamped so it can never exceed half the shorter side.
kg.node.rt_rounded_rectangle.in.uv: Coordinates; unconnected uses the mesh uv.
kg.node.rt_rounded_rectangle.note.1: Fragment-only, like the other shape masks.
kg.node.rt_polygon.desc.1: A mask of a regular polygon centered on the uv, with an anti-aliased edge.
kg.node.rt_polygon.in.uv: Coordinates; unconnected uses the mesh uv.
kg.node.rt_polygon.in.sides: Number of sides. Three gives a triangle, six a hexagon; large values approach a circle.
kg.node.rt_polygon.note.1: Fragment-only, like the other shape masks.
kg.node.rt_rounded_polygon.desc.1: A regular polygon whose corners are rounded off by an arc, anti-aliased. Built on an exact signed distance field, so the rounding is a true offset of the shape rather than an approximation.
kg.node.rt_rounded_polygon.in.uv: Coordinates; unconnected uses the mesh uv.
kg.node.rt_rounded_polygon.in.roundness: How much of each corner is replaced by an arc.
kg.node.rt_rounded_polygon.note.1: Fragment-only, like the other shape masks.
kg.node.rt_channel_mixer.desc.1: Rebuilds each output channel as a weighted mix of the input's red, green and blue. The three weight vectors default to the identity, so an unwired node passes the color through unchanged.
kg.node.rt_channel_mixer.in.red: How much R, G and B go into the output's red.
kg.node.rt_channel_mixer.in.green: How much R, G and B go into the output's green.
kg.node.rt_channel_mixer.in.blue: How much R, G and B go into the output's blue.
kg.node.rt_channel_mixer.example.1: Setting all three weight vectors to (0.33, 0.33, 0.33) gives a flat greyscale.
kg.node.rt_contrast.desc.1: Pushes colors away from mid-grey, or pulls them toward it. 1 leaves the color alone, above 1 hardens it, below 1 flattens it, and 0 collapses everything to grey.
kg.node.rt_contrast.note.1: The pivot is linear mid-grey, not 0.5, so the result matches what an image editor would do.
kg.node.rt_hue.desc.1: Rotates the color around the hue wheel, leaving how bright and how vivid it is untouched. Converts to HSV, shifts the hue, converts back.
kg.node.rt_hue.in.offset: The shift in degrees; it wraps, so 360 is a full turn back to the start.
kg.node.rt_hue.example.1: Time * 60 into offset cycles a color through the whole spectrum every six seconds.
kg.node.rt_invert_colors.desc.1: Inverts the channels you select and leaves the rest alone. The mask is per channel: 1 inverts, 0 keeps.
kg.node.rt_replace_color.desc.1: Swaps one color for another wherever the input is close enough to it — a chroma key. Everything outside the range is left untouched.
kg.node.rt_replace_color.in.to: The color to put in its place.
kg.node.rt_replace_color.in.range: How far from the target still counts as a match.
kg.node.rt_replace_color.in.fuzziness: How softly the replacement fades out past the range. 0 gives a hard cut.
kg.node.rt_saturation.desc.1: Pushes each channel away from the color's own brightness, or toward it. 1 leaves it alone, 0 gives greyscale, and above 1 oversaturates.
kg.node.rt_saturation.note.1: Brightness uses the Rec.709 weights, so green counts far more than blue — that is what keeps a desaturated image looking natural.
kg.node.rt_white_balance.desc.1: Warms or cools the image and shifts it between green and magenta, the same two controls a photo editor gives you.
kg.node.rt_white_balance.desc.2: It works by picking a white point and rebalancing in cone-response space rather than scaling RGB directly, which is why skin tones and neutrals survive the shift.
kg.node.rt_white_balance.in.temperature: Roughly -1 to 1. Positive warms toward orange, negative cools toward blue.
kg.node.rt_white_balance.in.tint: Roughly -1 to 1, shifting between green and magenta.
kg.node.rt_blend.desc.1: Combines two colors with a Photoshop-style blend mode, then fades from the base toward the result by opacity.
kg.node.rt_blend.desc.2: The mode is chosen at compile time, so only the formula you picked ends up in the shader — there is no runtime branch to pay for.
kg.node.rt_blend.in.opacity: How much of the blended result to apply. 0 gives the base back.
kg.node.rt_blend.note.1: Results are not clamped, matching Unity. Follow with Saturate if a mode can push channels out of range.
kg.node.rt_dither.desc.1: Subtracts a 4x4 ordered pattern that depends on the pixel's screen position. On its own it does almost nothing visible — the point is what happens when you threshold the result afterwards.
kg.node.rt_dither.desc.2: Thresholding a dithered value turns a smooth gradient into a stable screen-door pattern instead of a hard edge, which is how cutout fades and transparency-without-blending are usually done.
kg.node.rt_dither.example.1: Dither an alpha value and feed it into Alpha Discard for a fade that needs no blending and sorts correctly.
kg.node.rt_dither.note.1: Fragment-only, and the pattern is locked to screen pixels — so it stays put while the object moves behind it.
kg.node.rt_channel_mask.desc.1: Zeroes the channels you do not select. The mask is per channel: 1 keeps, 0 drops.
kg.node.rt_color_mask.desc.1: Produces a 0..1 mask that is 1 wherever the input is close to a target color, falling off past the range. The selection half of Replace Color.
kg.node.rt_color_mask.in.range: How far from the target still counts as a match.
kg.node.rt_color_mask.in.fuzziness: How softly the mask fades past the range.
kg.node.rt_normal_unpack.desc.1: Turns a normal-map texture sample into a real normal. Normal maps store directions squeezed into 0..1, so they have to be expanded back to -1..1 before they mean anything.
kg.node.rt_normal_unpack.note.1: Sample the normal map with a linear (non-sRGB) texture, otherwise the gamma curve bends the directions.
kg.node.rt_normal_strength.desc.1: Scales how pronounced a tangent-space normal is. 1 leaves it alone, 0 flattens it to face straight out, and above 1 exaggerates the bumps.
kg.node.rt_normal_blend.desc.1: Combines two tangent-space normals into one, using the whiteout method — so layering a detail normal over a base normal keeps both sets of bumps instead of one flattening the other.
kg.node.rt_normal_blend.in.b: The detail normal layered on top.
kg.node.rt_normal_reconstruct_z.desc.1: Rebuilds a normal's z from its x and y. Two-channel normal maps drop z to save space because a unit vector's third component is implied by the other two.
kg.node.rt_normal_reconstruct_z.in.in: The x and y of the normal.
kg.node.rt_normal_from_height.desc.1: Derives a normal from a height value by looking at how fast it changes across the screen. No height texture needed — it works on any float, including procedural noise.
kg.node.rt_normal_from_height.in.strengt: How pronounced the resulting bumps are.
kg.node.rt_normal_from_height.note.1: A screen-space approximation: the slopes are measured in pixels, so the apparent bumpiness changes with distance and zoom. Minecraft meshes carry no tangent basis, so a full reconstruction is not available.
kg.node.rt_normal_from_texture.desc.1: Builds a normal from a height texture by sampling it three times — at the uv and one small step along each axis — and crossing the two resulting slopes.
kg.node.rt_normal_from_texture.desc.2: Unlike Normal From Height this measures in texture space, so the bumpiness stays consistent regardless of how far away the surface is.
kg.node.rt_normal_from_texture.in.textur: The height texture; unconnected falls back to the missing-texture sampler.
kg.node.rt_normal_from_texture.in.uv: Where to sample; unconnected uses the mesh uv.
kg.node.rt_normal_from_texture.in.offset: How far apart the samples are taken, in uv units.
kg.node.rt_normal_from_texture.in.streng: How pronounced the resulting bumps are.
kg.node.rt_normal_from_texture.note.1: Three texture fetches per pixel, and fragment-only.
kg.node.rt_colorspace_conversion.desc.1: Converts a color between RGB, Linear and HSV. Everything routes through display RGB as the hub, so any pair of spaces works.
kg.node.rt_colorspace_conversion.desc.2: HSV is the useful one for color work: its x channel is hue, y is saturation and z is value, so shifting a single channel does exactly what you would expect.
RGB: display space, what a color picker gives you.
Linear: physically linear light, correct for blending and lighting math.
RGB: display space, what a color picker gives you.
Linear: physically linear light, correct for blending and lighting math.
kg.node.rt_colorspace_conversion.note.1: The sRGB and Linear conversion uses the common gamma 2.2 approximation rather than the exact piecewise curve.
kg.node.rt_sample_gradient.desc.1: Reads a color out of a Gradient at a position between 0 and 1. Color keys and alpha keys are interpolated separately, and the gradient's own mode decides whether the steps blend or snap.
kg.node.rt_sample_gradient.in.gradient: The gradient to sample, from a Gradient node or a Gradient variable.
kg.node.rt_sample_gradient.in.time: Where to sample, 0 to 1; unconnected sweeps across the mesh uv's x so the preview shows the whole gradient.
kg.node.rt_sample_gradient.example.1: A Fresnel value into time turns a gradient into a rim color ramp.
kg.node.rt_sample_curve.desc.1: Reads a float out of a Curve at a position between 0 and 1, remapped into the curve's own output range. The graphical way to shape a value without a chain of math nodes.
kg.node.rt_sample_curve.in.curve: The curve to sample, from a Curve node or a Curve variable.
kg.node.rt_sample_curve.in.time: Where to sample, 0 to 1; unconnected sweeps across the mesh uv's x so the preview shows the whole curve.
kg.node.rt_sample_curve.out.value: The sampled value, inside the curve's range.
kg.node.rt_sample_curve.example.1: Drive time from a linear Time node and let the curve do the easing, instead of assembling one out of Pow and Smoothstep.
kg.node.exec_entry.desc.1: The entry point of a blueprint's execution flow. It has no inputs — the host calls into it — and a single next output that fires the rest of the chain.
kg.node.exec_entry.out.next: Fires once when the run begins.
kg.node.exec_noop.tooltip: Does nothing and passes the flow through.
kg.node.exec_noop.desc.1: A pass-through with no behaviour. Useful purely for the shape of a graph: a tidy fan-in point where several branches meet, or a stable anchor to hang a breakpoint on.
kg.node.exec_branch.tooltip: The if statement: fires one of two outputs based on a condition.
kg.node.exec_branch.desc.1: Pulls the condition, then fires exactly one of the two exec outputs. Unlike the data-side Select node, this is real control flow — the branch not taken never runs.
kg.node.exec_branch.out.trueExec: Fires when the condition is true.
kg.node.exec_branch.out.falseExec: Fires when the condition is false.
kg.node.exec_gate.tooltip: Passes the flow through only while enabled.
kg.node.exec_gate.desc.1: Forwards the flow when enabled is true and drops it otherwise. A Branch with nothing wired to its false side, in one node.
kg.node.exec_gate.in.enabled: The flow continues only while this is true.
kg.node.exec_sequence.tooltip: Fires several outputs one after another, in order.
kg.node.exec_sequence.desc.1: Runs each output's chain to completion before starting the next, so the branches never interleave. That makes execution order something you can rely on, rather than an accident of how the engine happens to queue work.
kg.node.exec_sequence.desc.2: The outputs are named out1, out2 and so on; the option below decides how many there are.
kg.node.exec_sequence.option.outputs.too: How many outputs to fire, in order.
kg.node.exec_switch.tooltip: Fires one of N outputs chosen by an integer.
kg.node.exec_switch.desc.1: An N-way selector: selector 1 fires case1, 2 fires case2, and anything outside the range falls through to defaultExec. The usual way to build a state machine or a dispatch table.
kg.node.exec_switch.in.selector: Which case to fire, counting from 1.
kg.node.exec_switch.out.defaultExec: Fires when the selector matches no case.
kg.node.exec_switch.option.cases.tooltip: How many case outputs to offer.
kg.node.exec_switch.note.1: Cases are keyed by integer only. For string or enum dispatch, compare first and feed the index in.
kg.node.exec_for.tooltip: Counted loop: runs the body a fixed number of times.
kg.node.exec_for.desc.1: Fires body count times, publishing the current iteration on index, then fires completed once the loop finishes.
kg.node.exec_for.in.count: How many iterations to run. Zero or less skips the body entirely.
kg.node.exec_for.out.index: The current iteration, from 0 to count minus 1.
kg.node.exec_for.out.completed: Fires once, after the last iteration.
kg.node.exec_for.example.1: For with count 3, its body wired to Print and index wired to Print's value, logs 0, 1, 2.
kg.node.exec_for.note.1: Loops can nest: each keeps its own index, so an inner loop cannot clobber the outer one's.
kg.node.exec_foreach.tooltip: Loops over a list, one element at a time.
kg.node.exec_foreach.desc.1: Fires body once per element, exposing the element on item and its position on index, then fires completed.
kg.node.exec_foreach.in.list: The list to walk. An empty or missing list skips the body.
kg.node.exec_foreach.out.index: The current element's position, counting from 0.
kg.node.exec_foreach.out.completed: Fires once, after the last element.
kg.node.exec_while.tooltip: Loops while a condition stays true.
kg.node.exec_while.desc.1: Re-pulls the condition before every iteration, so anything the body changes is visible to the next test.
kg.node.exec_while.in.cond: Checked before each iteration; the loop stops as soon as it is false.
kg.node.exec_while.out.completed: Fires once the condition turns false, or the cap is hit.
Hard cap on iterations, so a condition that never turns false cannot hang the server.
kg.node.exec_while.note.1: The cap is a safety net, not a design tool. If a loop legitimately runs longer than the cap, raise it rather than relying on it to stop.
kg.node.exec_break.desc.1: Stops the innermost loop it sits inside and continues from that loop's completed output.
kg.node.exec_break.note.1: Placing it outside any loop is an error, reported when the graph runs.
kg.node.exec_continue.tooltip: Skips to the next iteration of the nearest enclosing loop.
kg.node.exec_continue.desc.1: Abandons the rest of the current iteration and starts the next one.
kg.node.exec_continue.note.1: Placing it outside any loop is an error, reported when the graph runs.
kg.node.exec_print.tooltip: Logs a value to the KilaGraph log.
kg.node.exec_print.desc.1: Writes the value to the log and remembers the most recent one, so tests and debugging tools can read it back without parsing log text. The blueprint equivalent of a print statement.
kg.node.exec_print.in.value: Anything. It is converted to text for the log.
kg.node.exec_assert.tooltip: Fails the run when a condition is not met.
kg.node.exec_assert.desc.1: Throws with the supplied message if the condition is false, and otherwise carries on. Use it to state an assumption you want caught loudly rather than silently producing a wrong result.
kg.node.exec_assert.in.condition: What must hold. False aborts the run.
kg.node.exec_assert.in.message: Text attached to the failure, so the log says what was expected.
kg.node.exec_set_var.tooltip: Writes a value into a graph variable.
kg.node.exec_set_var.desc.1: Stores the value under the named graph variable. Variables marked as outputs end up in the run's result map, which is how a blueprint hands data back to whatever invoked it.
kg.node.exec_set_var.note.1: Reading goes the other way, through a variable node on the data side — there is no Get Var exec node.
kg.node.exec_cache.tooltip: Computes a value once and reuses it for the rest of the run.
kg.node.exec_cache.desc.1: The first pull evaluates the input and stores the result; every later pull returns the stored copy. The value survives loop iterations, so an expensive computation that does not change can sit outside the work without being re-derived each time round.
kg.node.exec_cache.desc.2: It is a pure data node with no exec ports. To force a recompute, wire its ref output into a Cache Clear node.
kg.node.exec_cache.in.value: Evaluated once, on the first pull.
kg.node.exec_cache.out.ref: A handle to this cache, for Cache Clear.
kg.node.exec_cache.note.1: The cache lives for one run. A fresh run starts empty.
kg.node.exec_cache_clear.tooltip: Invalidates a Cache node so it recomputes.
kg.node.exec_cache_clear.desc.1: Clears the caches wired into ref, then continues. The next pull on those caches evaluates their input again.
kg.node.exec_cache_clear.in.ref: Which caches to clear. Leaving it unwired is a harmless no-op.
kg.node.exec_cache_clear.note.1: The ref wire is followed structurally rather than evaluated — pulling it would run the very cache that is about to be cleared.
kg.node.flow_select.tooltip: Picks one of two values based on a condition.
kg.node.flow_select.desc.1: The data-side ternary: out is ifTrue when the condition holds, ifFalse otherwise.
kg.node.flow_select.desc.2: Both sides are evaluated regardless of the condition. This selects a value, it does not skip work — for that, use the exec Branch node.
kg.node.flow_select.in.ifTrue: Used when the condition is true.
kg.node.flow_select.in.ifFalse: Used when the condition is false.
kg.node.flow_select.option.type.tooltip: The type carried by ifTrue, ifFalse and out.
kg.node.logic_and.tooltip: True only when every input is true.
kg.node.logic_and.desc.1: Folds all its inputs together with logical and. The option below sets how many inputs there are, so one node covers any arity.
kg.node.logic_and.out.out: True when every input is true.
kg.node.logic_or.tooltip: True when at least one input is true.
kg.node.logic_or.desc.1: Folds all its inputs together with logical or.
kg.node.logic_or.out.out: True when any input is true.
kg.node.logic_xor.tooltip: True when an odd number of inputs are true.
kg.node.logic_xor.desc.1: Folds all its inputs with exclusive or. With two inputs that reads as they differ; with more, it is a parity check.
kg.node.logic_xor.out.out: True when an odd number of inputs are true.
kg.node.logic_not.desc.1: True becomes false and false becomes true.
kg.node.logic_equals.tooltip: True when all inputs are equal.
kg.node.logic_equals.desc.1: Compares every input against the others for equality. It works on any type, not just numbers, so it also compares strings, items and block positions.
kg.node.logic_equals.out.out: True when all inputs are equal.
kg.node.logic_equals.note.1: Comparing floats for exact equality is unreliable. Test whether their difference is small instead.
kg.node.cmp_neq.tooltip: True when the two values differ.
kg.node.cmp_neq.desc.1: The inverse of Equals, over any type.
kg.node.cmp_lt.tooltip: True when a is less than b.
kg.node.cmp_le.tooltip: True when a is less than or equal to b.
kg.node.cmp_gt.tooltip: True when a is greater than b.
kg.node.cmp_ge.tooltip: True when a is greater than or equal to b.
kg.node.math_add.desc.1: Adds its inputs together. The option below sets how many there are, so one node covers two operands or ten.
kg.node.math_divide.note.1: Dividing by zero gives infinity or a not-a-number value, which then poisons everything downstream. Guard the divisor if it can reach zero.
kg.node.math_modulo.tooltip: The remainder of a divided by b.
kg.node.math_modulo.desc.1: What is left over after dividing. Handy for wrapping a counter into a range, or testing divisibility by comparing the result against 0.
kg.node.math_negate.desc.1: Positive becomes negative and negative becomes positive.
kg.node.math_abs.desc.1: Drops the sign, so -3 and 3 both give 3.
kg.node.math_sign.desc.1: Reports which side of zero the input is on, without its magnitude.
kg.node.math_sqrt.desc.1: The square root of the input.
kg.node.math_pow.tooltip: base raised to the power exp.
kg.node.math_pow.desc.1: Exponentiation. An exp of 0.5 is the square root; 2 squares the base.
kg.node.math_exp.tooltip: e raised to the power of the input.
kg.node.math_exp.desc.1: The natural exponential. Growth that compounds — the inverse of the natural logarithm.
kg.node.math_log.tooltip: Logarithm of the input, in a chosen base.
kg.node.math_log.desc.1: The power the base must be raised to in order to give the input. The base defaults to e, the natural logarithm.
kg.node.math_log.note.1: An input of zero or less yields 0 rather than failing.
kg.node.math_log_base.tooltip: Logarithm of a value in an arbitrary base.
kg.node.math_log_base.desc.1: Computed as log(value) divided by log(base), so any base works.
kg.node.math_log_base.in.value: The number to take the logarithm of.
kg.node.math_min.desc.1: Picks the smallest value. With two inputs it also serves as an upper bound.
kg.node.math_max.desc.1: Picks the largest value. With two inputs it also serves as a lower bound — the cheap way to keep a number above zero.
kg.node.math_clamp.tooltip: Keeps a value inside a range.
kg.node.math_clamp.desc.1: Returns the input, or the nearest end of the range when it falls outside.
kg.node.math_fract.tooltip: The part after the decimal point.
kg.node.math_fract.desc.1: Always lands in 0 up to but not including 1, so any input wraps into the unit range. The usual way to make a value repeat.
kg.node.math_lerp.tooltip: Blends from a to b by t.
kg.node.math_lerp.desc.1: Linear interpolation: t of 0 gives a, 1 gives b, and values in between blend proportionally.
kg.node.math_lerp.note.1: t is not clamped, so values outside 0 to 1 extrapolate beyond a and b.
kg.node.math_remap.tooltip: Rescales a value from one range into another.
